extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation featuring 39,553 paired top-bottom 360° images with corresponding depth and disparity maps, captured in dynamic indoor and outdoor human environments on a university campus under varied lighting and weather conditions. The dataset was collected using two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, and includes an augmented training set with increased label density via depth completion.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene; Jannik Endres; Albias Havolli; Charles Corbiere; Salim Cherkaoui; Alexandre Kontouli; Alexandre Alahi
extraction.citeAs: Zayene, Mehdi, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbiere, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, and Alexandre Alahi. HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335v2, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected across a university campus using a custom-built, remotely controlled robot chassis carrying a custom rig with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor. The dataset captures dynamic human pedestrian activity in indoor settings such as corridors and halls and outdoor settings such as squares, parking areas, roads, and footpaths, under varied lighting and weather conditions including day, end of day, and night. A central processor managed data capture and synchronization. The supplementary material states the dataset includes 26 video sequences captured between December 2023 and February 2024 at 10 Hz, while the main paper states 29 video sequences were collected.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Ground-truth depth labels are sparse because LiDAR point clouds cover only a fraction of the total pixels. The paper reports that original labels cover about 12% of pixels and that depth completion increases the ratio of labeled pixels to about 61%. Regions with insufficient nearby points, such as sky areas, are excluded, and labels outside the LiDAR vertical field of view are filtered out.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of synchronized top and bottom equirectangular images from two Ricoh Theta V cameras and LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 sensor mounted on the same rig. At the start of each recording, an external flash was used as a synchronization marker, and ROS timestamps were recorded for LiDAR data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Captured between December 2023 and February 2024; sequence dates listed from 2023-12-06 to 2024-01-27.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: LiDAR point clouds were projected onto bottom equirectangular images by selecting corresponding 3D LiDAR points and image pixels, applying initial rotation and translation transforms, converting to spherical coordinates, projecting to the equirectangular plane, and optimizing rotation and translation parameters with BFGS to minimize projection error. Depth values were converted to spherical disparity values. For augmented training data, temporally aggregated point clouds from the current frame plus four preceding and four succeeding frames were interpolated on spherical grid points using weighted averages of k-nearest neighbors, then filtered using uncertainty and out-of-distribution thresholds before mapping to the image.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Camera streams were synchronized with LiDAR using a flash trigger and ROS timestamps, then one out of every three camera frames was retained to match the LiDAR frame rate of 10 fps. Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps were cropped to remove unnecessary borders and sky/ground regions. The supplementary material states data were downsized from width 1024 to 512 for efficient training, while the main paper reports the resulting benchmark dataset at 1920×512 resolution after cropping. Test sequences were manually reviewed to ensure no overlap of scenes or areas with the train set. During model training, photometric data augmentation was applied for 360-IGEV-Stereo.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels were automatically generated by projecting synchronized LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images after calibration and optimization of the LiDAR-to-image mapping. At the beginning of each recorded session, a set of key 3D points on a 19x19 chessboard was manually selected in the LiDAR scans and corresponding image pixel positions were manually selected in the bottom equirectangular image for calibration. An augmented training set was created using a fully automated depth completion pipeline that temporally aggregates neighboring point clouds, interpolates depth on spherical grid points using k-nearest neighbors, and filters uncertain or out-of-distribution points.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Alignment accuracy was assessed by measuring Euclidean pixel error between projected LiDAR points and manually selected corresponding image positions. The paper reports an average error of 1.7 pixels for 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and 8.0 pixels for visually challenging areas such as object edges. For depth completion, the method was validated using an 80-20 split of each LiDAR point cloud into training and test sets and evaluated with MAE, RMSE, MARE, Inlier Ratio, Actual Ratio of Interpolated Points, and Ratio of Labeled Pixels. Filtering based on relative weighted variance and neighbor-distance thresholds was used to avoid uncertain or out-of-distribution labels.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: BFGS optimization; depth completion pipeline; KISS-ICP evaluated for temporal aggregation comparison but not used in final pipeline
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Human presence and pedestrian counts in recorded scenes
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper frames the dataset as supporting research on robotic navigation and interaction in dynamic human environments and states that it is an ideal testbed for assessing the robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges. It also emphasizes the importance of evaluating generalization to unseen or underrepresented conditions, such as outdoor environments at night, for safe deployment in real-world settings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset was collected on a university campus, and the paper notes that it captures common urban environments such as parking lots, roads, underpasses, pedestrian squares, footpaths, corridors, and crowded halls. The authors analyze cross-scene generalization and report that models trained on specific environments generalize poorly to others, particularly indoor-trained models on outdoor night scenes. The supplementary material notes a concentration of short-range distances in the 0-10 meter range and an exponential decay in pixel percentage with increasing depth due to LiDAR precision decreasing over longer distances. Depth completion increases the density of low-range depth values, especially within 0-10 meters.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes several limitations: LiDAR depth labels are sparse; fast-moving objects like cars are a limitation for the temporal aggregation used in depth completion; object boundaries are difficult to label precisely from depth data alone; regions with insufficient nearby points such as sky areas are excluded; occlusions were not explicitly handled, though the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact; and indoor-trained models show limited generalization to outdoor scenes, particularly at night. The supplementary material also notes that evaluation of depth completion on point-cloud splits may underestimate actual image-based errors due to distribution shift.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for developing, training, benchmarking, and evaluating omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models. It includes train, validation, and test splits, and an augmented training set produced by depth completion to increase label density for training. The paper uses it to benchmark stereo depth estimation methods, study cross-scene generalization, and assess robustness to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges.
